record.file_problem: none; the full post and comments are present
record.tranche_reason: The study compares SAEs of different widths and examines feature similarities and additions, testing size-related feature relationships with decoder cosine similarity and reconstruction effects rather than the original masked-activation measure.
record.gate_note: The post reports size comparisons, cosine similarities, feature additions and swaps, and a weekday split in an author comment. SAE reconstruction-quality results are included only where they report an outcome of adding or swapping features or characterize cross-size feature relationships. The described figures do not provide extractable numerical values unless the text states them.
record.test_reason: The post compares GPT-2 SAEs of different widths at one site using decoder cosine similarity, feature addition and swaps. It reports how many larger-SAE features are splits of smaller-SAE features versus novel ones. That bears on V1, V3 and V5 with a method other than the original masked-activation one.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that wider SAEs learn reconstruction features (identical or split; cosine >0.7; about 65%) that mainly sparsify existing information, and novel features (about 35%) carrying new information. Adding novel features improves smaller SAEs. Stitched 'Frankenstein' SAEs get lower MSE at equal size but much higher L0.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE width comparisons like the feature-splitting work, but identifies relationships primarily through decoder cosine similarity and feature-addition or swap effects rather than measuring whether activations partition across split features. It uses a 0.7 similarity threshold and does not directly quantify parent-input coverage.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature categorization depends on decoder cosine similarity and the somewhat arbitrary 0.7 threshold. The authors say results may not generalize beyond the tested architectures, layers, and training setups.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors argue that high-similarity 'reconstruction features' mainly reduce the sparsity term while novel features reduce MSE. This assigns splitting to the L1 objective but is not tested against alternative objectives.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Split features in wider SAEs trade sparsity for reconstruction, while novel features trade reconstruction for capacity.

record.problems: The authors describe the cosine metric and 0.7 threshold as somewhat arbitrary; they say generalization is unclear and note that much larger models and MLP or attention layers were not tested. The study does not quantify whether child features partition parent-feature inputs. Numerical uncertainty estimates are not reported, and several outcomes are described qualitatively or in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were omitted.

untested.parts: Whether child features partition or jointly cover the parent's inputs. Cosine similarity is a proxy validated only by R² 0.87 with the masked-activation metric.
Large models and multiple open SAE families. Only GPT-2 small and Pythia-410M were used, and the Pythia results are unquantified.
Whether families mirror a concept hierarchy in the model. Nesting across more than two sizes is shown only anecdotally (weekday comment).
All; no parent/child firing gaps are measured.
Whether larger latents decompose into combinations of smaller latents. Matching uses max cosine to a single feature. No claim is tested that no size is complete or atomic.
All. The authors only assert that reconstruction features 'mostly reduce the sparsity component'; there is no Matryoshka or objective comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Written by Bussmann and Leask, a precursor to the original source arXiv:2502.04878, but a separate document, so verdicts are given. The 0.7 threshold is described as somewhat arbitrary. Family membership and 'near direction' are defined by the same cosine measure, so V1 and V3 support is partly by construction. The weekday evidence is from author comments. The Frankenstein results are the post's own method performance and are not recorded as claim rows.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not directly test whether child features partition the coarse feature's inputs or quantify their combined input coverage.
It uses GPT-2 and Pythia-410M-deduped SAEs, but does not test large models or the claim across open SAE releases.
It identifies cross-size feature families and gives a weekday example, but does not establish nested families across multiple sizes or show that the families mirror a general hierarchy of concepts.
The study does not test parent-child activation gaps or whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes them.

It identifies novel larger-SAE features and similar or split features, but does not demonstrate that larger latents decompose into combinations of smaller latents or establish that no size yields a complete atomic set.
It does not test whether the SAE objective causes splitting on correlated or hierarchical inputs, or compare with Matryoshka SAEs.
